---
title: "A small MLP neural network for autonomous obstacle avoidance"
---

## AI Model

A realistic example of an AI agent running directly on a microcontroller will be given here.

Application: A two-wheel autonomous robot that moves through a room and avoids obstacles.

**Model**: A small fully connected neural network (MLP) that receives distance measurements and predicts the safest movement direction.

A practical starting architecture could be:

$$\boxed{3\rightarrow 16 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 2}$$

- 3 inputs: Left, front, and right distances measurements
- 16 neurons: First hidden layer
- 8 neurons: Second hidden layer
- 2 outputs: Steering and speed

The model would be trained on a computer and deployed to the STM32 using X-CUBE-AI.
In this model, a small fully connected neural network (MLP) that receives distance measurements and predicts the safest movement direction is applied. 
ST provides tools for optimizing neural networks and generating C code for STM32 devices.

## The Concrete robot definition ##
To provide the dataset the concrete definition  of the robot should be determined. It is a custome robot with the properties given in @tbl-Parameters.

| Parameter                |                                                      Value |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------: |
| Drive type               |                                         Differential drive |
| Wheel separation \(L\)   |                                                     0.16 m |
| Wheel radius \(r\)       |                                                    0.032 m |
| Maximum wheel speed      |                                                   0.60 m/s |
| Maximum robot speed      |                                                   0.40 m/s |
| Maximum angular velocity |                                                  2.5 rad/s |
| Sensor range             |                                                0.05–2.00 m |
| Sensors                  |                                                3 × VL53L0X |
| Sensor directions        | Left \($−45^\circ$\), Front \($0^\circ$\), Right \($+45^\circ$\) |
: The parameters of a custom robot {#tbl-Parameters}

The three sensors measure $d_L​,d_F​,d_R$.
It is recommended that the neural network learn two physical control variables:​
$[d_L​,d_F​,d_R]\rightarrow [v_d,\omega_d]$
Where<br> 
$v_d$: desired linear velocity [m/s].<br>
$\omega_d$: desired angular velocity [rad/s].<br>

This is a better selection because the $v_d,\omega_d$ has a direct physical meaning.
At first, a reference controller is created. This controller is not an AI. It is used to generate physically meaningful training data, For example, define:
$$
v_d =
\begin{cases}
0, & d_F \leq 0.2 \\
0.4.\frac{d_F-0.2}{0.8-0.2}, & 0.2<x < 0.8 \\
0.4, & d_F > 0.8
\end{cases}
$$

Thus:<br>
obstacle very close → stop<br>
obstacle moderately close → slow down<br>
obstacle far away → move at up to 0.40 m/s<br>

**Desired turning rate**<br>
We can define the desired angular velocity from the difference between left and right distances: 
$e_d​=d_L​−d_R$
and 
$$
\omega_d=K_{\omega_d}.\frac{d_L​−d_R}{d_L​+d_R}
$$
with saturation like:
$$ -2.5\leq\omega_d\leq2.5 $$

Here is defined:<br>
<center> $\omega>0 \Rightarrow \text{turn left}$<br>
$\omega<0 \Rightarrow \text{turn right}$ </center>
Therefore, if: $$ d_R>d_L $$ then: $$ d_L-d_R<0 $$<br>
and therefore:<br>
$$ \omega_d<0 $$
So the robot turns right, toward the wider space. This fixes the inconsistency we had earlier, since physical definition get improved.

**Convert the desired motion into actual wheel velocities**

This is where the robot physics enters to the problem.

For a differential-drive robot:
$$ v=\frac{v_R+v_L}{2} $$ and: $$ \omega=\frac{v_R-v_L}{L} $$
Therefore:<br>
<center>$\boxed{ v_L=v_d-\frac{L}{2}\omega_d }$
$\boxed{ v_R=v_d+\frac{L}{2}\omega_d }$ </center><br>
With $L=0.16\,m$, we get:<br>
$$v_L=v_d-0.08\omega_d $$ $$ v_R=v_d+0.08\omega_d$$

Then we impose the motor limits:<br>
$$ -0.60\leq v_L,v_R\leq0.60 $$

This is a physically meaningful training target.

Besides, it is also needed to consider the front obstacle.

Suppose:

$$ d_L=1.2\,m $$ $$ d_F=0.25\,m $$ $$ d_R=0.4\,m $$

The front obstacle is very close.

Simply using $(d_L-d_R)$ isn't enough, because the robot needs to make a stronger avoidance maneuver. Therefore, a better reference controller is:

$$ \omega_d = K_1\frac{d_L-d_R}{d_L+d_R} + K_2\left(\frac{1}{d_F}-\frac{1}{d_F^{ref}}\right) \operatorname{sign}(d_L-d_R) $$

with appropriate saturation.

This makes the turning response stronger when the front obstacle becomes close.

For a first implementation, however,the controller is kept simpler and validated experimentally before adding complexity.

**A correct training sample**<br>
Suppose the sensors measure:
$$ d_L=0.80\,m $$ $$ d_F=1.20\,m $$ $$ d_R=1.20\,m $$
Since the front is clear:
$$ v_d=0.40\,m/s $$

and:

$$ d_L-d_R=0 $$

therefore:

$$ \omega_d=0 $$

So:

$$ v_L=v_R=0.40\,m/s $$

The robot goes straight.<br>

**The training dataset**<br>
These data should be gathered in a csv file:<br>
[d_left_m, d_front_m, d_right_m, v_desired_mps, omega_desired_radps]
<br>
However, the numbers in csv file should not be treated as the final dataset yet. A proper dataset should be generated automatically from the reference controller over thousands of physically possible sensor states.

![MLP Neural Network for the AI model](../imagescopy/picture2.jpg){
  #fig-NNMLP
  fig-cap="The MLP Neural Network of the AI-model"
  fig-alt="MLP neural network diagram"
}

The project would be now defined as:

$$ \boxed{ \text{VL53L0X} \rightarrow \text{MLP} \rightarrow (v_d,\omega_d) \rightarrow (v_L,v_R) \rightarrow \text{PWM} \rightarrow \text{motors} } $$

with:

$$ \boxed{ \text{MLP}:3\rightarrow32\rightarrow16\rightarrow2 } $$

and:

$$ \boxed{ \text{Input}=[d_L,d_F,d_R]\quad[m] } $$ $$ \boxed{ \text{Output}=[v_d,\omega_d]\quad[m/s,\ rad/s] } $$

Then:

$$ \boxed{ v_L=v_d-\frac{L}{2}\omega_d } $$ $$ \boxed{ v_R=v_d+\frac{L}{2}\omega_d } $$

This is substantially more physically defensible than the original normalized steering/speed example.<br>

**Updated project workflow**<br>

1. Define the robot<br>
- STM32
- Differential-drive, two DC motors
- Wheel radius, wheel separation, maximum wheel speed
2. Select sensors<br>
- $d_L,d_F,d_R$ from the three VL53L0X ToF sensors
3. Implement sensor acquisition<br>
- STM32 I²C
- Distance values in meters
4. Implement motor control<br>
- PWM
- Differential-drive equations

5. Define the physical robot model<br>

- $$ v=\frac{v_R+v_L}{2} $$ $$ \omega=\frac{v_R-v_L}{L} $$
6. Develop the reference obstacle-avoidance controller
- Produces physically valid \(v_d,\omega_d\)

7. Generate the training dataset

- $$ [d_L,d_F,d_R]\rightarrow[v_d,\omega_d] $$
- Floating-point data
- Physically possible sensor states
- Labels generated by the reference controller

8. Train the MLP neural network

- $$ 3\rightarrow32\rightarrow16\rightarrow2 $$ 
- FP32 training
9. Validate the FP32 MLP
- Prediction error
- Obstacle-avoidance behavior
- Check against physical constraints
10. Quantize the trained MLP ← THIS IS WHERE QUANTIZATION GOES
11. Validate the quantized MLP
- Compare FP32 vs INT8 outputs
- Check whether quantization changes robot behavior significantly
12. Deploy the quantized MLP to STM32
- STM32Cube.AI / STM32Cube AI Studio
- Generate optimized C code
13. Integrate MLP with FreeRTOS
- Sensor task
- AI inference task
- Motor-control task
- Safety task
14. Run the real robot
15. Measure real-time performance
- Inference time
- CPU utilization
- RAM/Flash
- Task execution time
- Deadline misses
- End-to-end latency
16. Evaluate navigation performance
- Collision rate
- Completion rate
- Path efficiency
- Average velocity
- Energy consumption


## Overall architecture ##
For the custom robot, the MLP should be integrated with FreeRTOS as a pipeline of periodic tasks, with the Safety task having the highest priority.
The key idea is that the MLP should not directly control the motors. It produces a desired command, and the safety and motor-control layers decide whether and how that command is actually applied.
The Figure 4 illustrate this integration.

![The overal archtecture of the integration of FreeRTOS with MLP](../imagescopy/picture4.jpg){#fig-integration fig-alt="Integration of RTOS and MLP"}

**SensorTask**

The SensorTask periodically reads the three VL53L0X sensors.
For example:
$$ T_S=20\,ms $$
which corresponds to:
$$ f_S=50\,Hz. $$

It reads $d_L, d_F, d_R$ and stores them in a shared sensor structure.

**AI inference task**

The AITask reads the latest sensor vector:

$$ X= \begin{bmatrix} d_L\\ d_F\\ d_R \end{bmatrix} $$

and feeds it to:

$$ \boxed{3\rightarrow8\rightarrow16\rightarrow2} $$

The MLP generates:

<center>$Y=[v_d, \omega_d]$</center>

Then constrain the output:

$$ 0\leq v_d\leq0.40\,m/s \ and -2.5\leq\omega_d\leq2.5\,rad/s $$

For our previously defined custom robot, the AITask could initially run every $T_{AI}=20\,ms$, but 20 ms is a starting design value, not a measured requirement.
The neural network should never have unrestricted authority over the motors.

**The SafetyTask**<br>
The saftey task independently checks the sensor data. For example:
$d_F < 0.10\,m$ means: 
$$ \boxed{v_d=0,\quad\omega_d=0} $$

regardless of what the MLP says. We could have several safety levels:

Emergency<center> $d_F < 0.10m$ → immediate stop.</center><br>
Danger <center>$0.10\leq d_F<0.20m$ → force: $v_d=0.$<br></center>
Normal <center>$d_F≥0.20m$ → allow the AI command, subject to limits.</center>


**MotorTask**

The MotorTask converts $v_d,\omega_d$ into left/right wheel velocities.

For our differential-drive robot:
$$ v_L=v_d-\frac{L}{2}\omega_d $$ $$ v_R=v_d+\frac{L}{2}\omega_d. $$

With $L=0.16\ m$ we have:
$$ \boxed{v_L=v_d-0.08\omega_d} $$ $$ \boxed{v_R=v_d+0.08\omega_d}. $$

Then convert wheel velocity to motor commands/PWM. In a better implementation, the motor task would use wheel encoders and closed-loop velocity control, rather than mapping velocity directly to PWM.<br>

**FreeRTOS priorities**

Priorities would be initially assigned like @tbl-Tasks.

| Task       | Period | Priority | Function                     |
| ---------- | -----: | -------: | ---------------------------- |
| SafetyTask |   5 ms |    **4** | Emergency/safety supervision |
| MotorTask  |   5 ms |    **3** | Wheel control/PWM            |
| SensorTask |  20 ms |    **2** | Read ToF sensors             |
| AITask     |  20 ms |    **2** | MLP inference                |
: The tasks schedule {#tbl-Tasks}


The exact priorities should eventually be determined from the measured execution times and timing requirements, rather than assumed.

The important hierarchy is:

$$ \boxed{ Safety > Motor > AI/Sensor } $$

because an AI inference task should never prevent an emergency stop.


## Agent

The agent is the complete autonomous robot,the RTOS coordinates these tasks, while the AI model helps determine the robot's action.

::: {.text-center}
**Agent**

STM32 + RTOS + Sensors + AI + Motor Control

sensor task $\rightarrow$ AI inference task $\rightarrow$ decision task $\rightarrow$ motor control
:::

### The complete interaction loop

<!--![The complete interaction loop](../images/picture3.jpg){
  #fig-loop
  fig-cap="The complete interaction loop"
  fig-alt="Interaction loop"
}!-->

<!--![The complete interaction loop](../images/picture3.jpg){#fig-loop fig-alt="Interaction loop"}!-->

Mathematically:

- AI Model: $s_t \rightarrow a_t$
- Environment: $(s_t, a_t) \rightarrow s_{t+1}$

Where:

- $(s_t)$: current sensor state
- $(a_t)$: Robot action
- $(s_{t+1})$: New sensor state

For example:

$$[0.80,\ 0.25,\ 1.00] \rightarrow [-0.65,\ 0.20] \rightarrow [0.60,\ 0.35,\ 0.95]$$

The robot has turned left, so the next sensor measurements are different.
![The complete interaction loop](../imagescopy/picture3.jpg){
  #fig-loop
  fig-cap="The complete interaction loop"
  fig-alt="Interaction loop"
}

The RTOS coordinates these tasks, while the AI model helps determine the robot's action.


Suppose the robot has three distance sensors:

::: {.text-center}
left = 80 cm, front = 25 cm, right = 100 cm, with quantization of 200: $distance=initial\ distance/200$:
:::
$$x=[0.4,\ 0.125,\ 0.5]^T$$

Hence,the values are normalized before being given to the neural network.
The model might produce:

$$y=[+0.7,\ 0.25]^T$$

Where:

- Steering = +0.65: Turn right
- Speed = 0.25: Move slowly (25% of maximum speed)

The robot then converts these outputs into motor commands.
The model does not directly control the motors. It produces a decision that the control software interprets.<br>

## Environment

The neural network is the decision-making model; the agent is the complete robot system that uses the model.

The environment is the physical world surrounding the robot. In this specific AI model, the components are:

- Walls
- Tables
- Chairs
- People
- Other obstacles
- Floor surface
- Battery and motor conditions

The environment changes when the robot moves.

![A two-wheel autonomous robot](../imagescopy/picture1.jpg){#fig-robot fig-alt="Two-wheel robot"}
